h1: Keeping a sensory journal that sharpens your palate over months
title: A Sensory Journal for a Sharper Palate | Craft Beer School
desc: How to keep a beer sensory journal that actually trains your palate: what to record, how to score and how to review it so you improve.
teaser: Most tasting notes end up as a list of beers you once drank. A good journal turns them into a training record.
standfirst: Writing down what you taste is the single cheapest way to get better at tasting. The trick is to record the right things in the same way every time. Then you read the notes back. Done well, a journal shows your palate improving month by month.
sections:
Memory for flavour is short and unreliable. A beer you loved in March becomes simply good by June. The details are gone. Writing forces you to pay attention while you taste, to choose specific words and to commit to a judgement you can check later.

Professional panels keep records for exactly this reason. A taster's scores over months show where they are reliable, where they drift and which faults they miss. You can do the same for yourself with a notebook or a spreadsheet.

Keep the format fixed. The same headings every time make entries comparable. A practical set:

  • Basics: date, beer, brewery, style, ABV, pack date or best before if printed.
  • Serving: can, bottle or draught, glass type and roughly how cold.
  • Appearance: colour, clarity, foam.
  • Aroma: the first three things you smell, as specific as you can.
  • Flavour: malt, hops, yeast character, sweetness, bitterness.
  • Mouthfeel: body, carbonation, warmth, astringency.
  • Finish: character and length in seconds.
  • Faults: anything off, with a confidence level.
  • Overall: a score and one sentence.

Our simple beer tasting sheet is a ready template if you want one to start with.

Writing hoppy is a start. Writing hop aroma 4 out of 5, citrus and pine is far more useful. Use a simple 0 to 5 intensity scale for the main attributes: malt sweetness, bitterness, hop aroma, fruitiness, body and carbonation. Keep the scale the same across entries.

Intensity scores let you compare beers months apart and see your own habits. You might find that you always score bitterness high, or that your body scores jump around for the same beer. Both tell you where to practise. A spreadsheet makes this easy, because you can sort and chart the scores, but a notebook works if you are disciplined.

Many apparent changes in a beer are really changes in the setting. The same IPA tastes different from a cold can at home and from a warm glass on a terrace in May. Note the temperature, the food you had with it, the time of day and how tired you were.

Also note freshness. Hop aroma fades over weeks, faster in heat. An Indian summer without proper cold storage can take the edge off an IPA well before its best before date. If your notes for the same beer change, check the pack date before you blame your palate.

A journal you never read does little. Set aside half an hour once a month to read the last month's entries. Look for patterns:

  • Words you use too often. If everything is fruity, push for pear, apricot or mango.
  • Attributes you never mention. If you never note carbonation, start paying attention to it.
  • Beers you tasted twice. Do your notes agree? If not, why?
  • Faults you flagged. Were you right? Did others notice the same?

Every few months, retaste a beer you know well, write fresh notes without looking back and then compare. The difference between the two entries is your progress, in writing.

A journal kept alone can drift. You may settle into describing every lager the same way, or keep missing a fault you have never been shown. Tasting the same beer with one or two friends now and then, each writing notes before talking, is a simple check.

Compare the three sets of notes afterwards. Where you all agree, your palate is probably calibrated. Where one person found something the others missed, go back to the glass and look for it. Over a few months these sessions show you which attributes you are strong on and which you need to practise. Keep the pours small and have water on the table.

A journal becomes much more powerful once you start tying words to real references. When you smell clove in a hefeweizen, note it, then smell an actual clove the next day and decide whether you were right. When a beer seems buttery, look for a known example of diacetyl to compare. Our guide on training your palate covers building that reference library.

Breweries do the same at scale by picking reference beers that anchor a panel. A personal journal is the home version of that discipline. Over months it becomes your own flavour dictionary, built from beers you have actually tasted.

Open a notebook or a spreadsheet tonight and write the nine headings above. Taste one beer with care and fill every heading, even the ones that feel hard. Do it again for the next four beers you drink. At the end of the month, read all five entries back in one sitting.
faqs: What should a beer tasting journal include?
Basics such as beer, style and pack date, serving details, appearance, aroma, flavour, mouthfeel, finish, faults and an overall score, recorded in the same format each time.
How often should I review my tasting notes?
Once a month works well. Look for overused words, attributes you never mention and beers you tasted twice to check whether your notes agree.
Should I use a notebook or a spreadsheet?
Either works. A spreadsheet makes it easier to sort and chart intensity scores, while a notebook is quicker at the table. Pick the one you will actually use.
